cards.definition: Traditional: data plus rules give answers. ML: data plus answers give the rules (the model).
cards.useCase: Use ML when the rules are too many or too hard to write by hand.
cards.example: A learned miles-to-km line instead of a typed formula

cards.definition: A number from -1 to +1 showing how two variables move together.
cards.useCase: Check it to see whether one variable could help predict another.

cards.definition: Regression that predicts a value from two or more inputs, each with its own coefficient.
cards.useCase: Use it when one input is not enough to predict a number.
cards.example: Price from area, age and bedrooms

cards.definition: A model that outputs a probability compared with a threshold; used for binary classification.
cards.useCase: Use it for yes/no predictions.

cards.definition: Machine learning with neural networks that have 2 or more hidden layers.
cards.useCase: Use it when features are hard to hand-pick, as with images.
cards.example: Each layer's output feeds the next layer

cards.definition: Labelled data split into a training set (about 70-80%) and a test set (about 20-30%).
cards.useCase: Train on the first, check accuracy on the second.

cards.definition: A classifier that finds a boundary between classes using the points nearest it, the support vectors.
cards.useCase: Good in high-dimensional data; kernels allow curved boundaries.

cards.definition: The training points that define the SVM boundary.
cards.useCase: Only these points are kept in the decision function, so SVMs are memory efficient.
cards.example: The points closest to the dividing line

cards.definition: Classes are linearly separable when a straight line or plane can split them.
cards.useCase: Tells you whether a linear model can work.
cards.example: Two blobs on opposite sides of a line

cards.definition: A classic dataset: 150 flowers, 3 species (labels), 4 measurements in cm (features).
cards.useCase: Practice for classification and clustering.
cards.example: Features: sepal and petal length and width

cards.definition: TP and TN are correct predictions; FP is a negative called positive; FN is a positive called negative.
cards.useCase: Read them from the confusion matrix.

cards.definition: Splitting the data into k folds, using each as the test set once, and scoring k models.
cards.useCase: Gives a steadier accuracy estimate than a single split.
cards.example: 5 folds on 500 rows: 400 train, 100 test each round

cards.definition: How well a model performs on examples it did not see in training.
cards.useCase: Measured by test accuracy.

cards.definition: The model memorizes the training set and its noise: high training accuracy, low test accuracy.
cards.useCase: Fix with regularization, fewer features or more data.

cards.definition: The model is too simple to capture the pattern: low accuracy on training and test sets.
cards.useCase: Fix with a more flexible model or better features.

cards.definition: Clustering by distance to cluster centres that are moved to fit the data. Example: k-means.
cards.useCase: Use it when you know roughly how many groups you want.

cards.definition: Connectivity-based clustering that joins points step by step into a tree of clusters.
cards.useCase: Use it when you want to see how groups nest.
cards.example: Merging the two closest points, then groups

cards.definition: Density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise: groups points that are densely packed.
cards.useCase: Use it for odd-shaped clusters and to flag noise points.
cards.example: A dense ring of points becomes one cluster

cards.definition: The straight-line distance between two points: the square root of the squared differences added up.
cards.useCase: The usual distance for clustering and kNN.

cards.definition: The sum of the horizontal and vertical differences, like walking a street grid.
cards.useCase: Cheaper to compute but less precise than Euclidean.

cards.definition: Load, explore, transform, split, create, train and test, tune, predict on live data, monitor.
cards.useCase: Follow in order; the split comes before training.
cards.example: Load CSV -> explore -> encode -> split -> fit

cards.definition: Convert non-numeric data into numbers, because scikit-learn requires numeric input.
cards.useCase: Do it before splitting and fitting.

cards.definition: fit trains the model, predict returns labels for new inputs, accuracy_score compares them with the real labels.
cards.useCase: The three calls of the scikit-learn pattern.

cards.definition: A scikit-learn function that splits data into training and test sets.
cards.useCase: Set test_size to the share held back.

cards.definition: Periodically evaluate the deployed model and tune, retrain or redeploy if needed.
cards.useCase: Do it because real-world data changes.
cards.example: Accuracy slowly drops after a year

cards.definition: Removing inputs that do not help the model.
cards.useCase: Saves time and memory and often improves results.
cards.example: Dropping a column that never changes

cards.definition: Scores features by their own characteristics, without training a model.
cards.useCase: A quick screen for irrelevant features.

cards.definition: Trains a model on feature subsets and scores them: very effective but computationally intensive.
cards.useCase: Use it when accuracy matters more than speed.

cards.definition: Feature selection built into model training; fits the model once.
cards.useCase: A balance between filter and wrapper.

cards.definition: A wrapper that repeatedly builds models, drops the weakest feature, and ranks features by elimination order.
cards.useCase: Use it for a thorough ranking.

cards.definition: Cutting the number of features (dimensions) while keeping the useful information.
cards.useCase: Reduces processing time and memory.
cards.example: Dropping LD2 when LD1 separates the classes

cards.definition: Principal component analysis: an unsupervised method that maps features onto fewer dimensions with maximum variance.
cards.useCase: Use it to compress features without labels.
cards.example: Ten measurements reduced to two components

cards.definition: Linear discriminant analysis: a supervised method that finds the axes that best separate classes.
cards.useCase: Use it when labels are available.

cards.definition: Another word for a feature or input.
cards.useCase: Remember: dimensions = features = inputs.
cards.example: A dataset with 57 columns has 57 dimensions

cards.definition: Converting a continuous value into two classes at a threshold.
cards.useCase: Use it when only above-or-below matters.

cards.definition: Grouping continuous values into ranges (bins).
cards.useCase: Use it to turn a number into a few categories.

cards.definition: Turning each category into its own 0/1 column.
cards.useCase: Use it for text categories so no false order is implied.

cards.definition: Numbering categories implies an order that does not exist.
cards.useCase: Avoid ordinal numbers for unordered categories.

cards.definition: The pandas function that one-hot encodes a column.
cards.useCase: Call it on the categorical column.

cards.definition: Putting attributes on comparable scales.
cards.useCase: Do it for distance-based algorithms such as kNN.

cards.definition: Rescaling values into the range 0 to 1: (x - min) / (max - min).
cards.useCase: Use it when the distribution is unknown or not Gaussian.

cards.definition: Rescaling to mean 0 and standard deviation 1: (x - mean) / standard deviation.
cards.useCase: Use it when the algorithm assumes normal data.

cards.definition: Normalization gives a 0-1 range; standardization centres on 0 with variance 1.
cards.useCase: Choose by the algorithm and the data's distribution.

cards.definition: Penalizing large weights so a model stops fitting noise, balancing bias and variance.
cards.useCase: Use it to reduce overfitting.

cards.definition: Regularization that can push coefficients to exactly zero, removing features.
cards.useCase: Use it for feature selection as well as regularization.

cards.definition: Regularization that shrinks weights but keeps most or all features.
cards.useCase: Use it to smooth out outliers without dropping features.
cards.example: Many small weights, none exactly zero
